title: Periodontal risk factors & systemic links
blurb: Why the same plaque does more damage in some patients: smoking, diabetes and other risk factors, the links with general health, and what to record.
question: A 52-year-old patient smokes 20 cigarettes a day and has type 2 diabetes that his GP says is not well controlled. His gums look pale and barely bleed, yet the dentist finds deep pockets and bone loss. Why don't his gums look as bad as they are, which risk factors should be recorded, and how is his mouth linked to his general health?

teach.h: Plaque causes it; risk factors decide how bad it gets
teach.body: Plaque bacteria are the primary cause of periodontal disease. But two people with the same amount of plaque can end up very differently: one has mild gingivitis, the other loses teeth. The difference is how each person's body responds. Risk factors change that response, making breakdown faster, healing slower and treatment less successful. The highest-risk patient is a smoker with poor plaque control. Spotting and recording risk factors helps the dentist plan care and target advice.

children.label: Modifiable
children.sub: Smoking, plaque control, diabetes control, attendance, stress

children.label: Non-modifiable
children.sub: Genetics and family history, increasing age

teach.caption: Prevention focuses on the modifiable factors. Non-modifiable ones tell the team who needs closer monitoring.

teach.h: Smoking: the biggest modifiable risk factor
teach.body: Smoking narrows the blood vessels in the gums and weakens the immune defence. Smokers get deeper pockets, more bone loss and more tooth loss, and they heal and respond to treatment less well. Because blood flow is reduced, the gums bleed less and can look pale and firm. Smoking hides the warning signs while the disease gets worse underneath. Stopping smoking improves the response to periodontal treatment.

teach.h: What smoking does to the picture

teach.caption: Brown tobacco staining and deposits at the gum margins of the lower teeth. Remember that smoking can mask redness and bleeding, so a smoker's gums may look healthier than they are. The white patch on the lower lip should also be pointed out to the dentist.

teach.body: Poorly controlled diabetes alters the immune response and slows healing, so periodontitis is more common, more severe and progresses faster. The link works both ways: periodontal inflammation makes blood glucose harder to control, and successful periodontal treatment can help improve it. Patients whose diabetes is well controlled carry much less extra risk. That's why the medical history should record not just 'diabetes' but how well it is controlled.

teach.h: Diabetes and gum disease feed each other
Other risk factors and systemic links
head: Factor
Link with gum disease
rows: Hormones worsen gingivitis; periodontitis linked with preterm, low-birth-weight babies
Plaque bacteria can be inhaled (aspiration pneumonia) in frail patients
Gum overgrowth (phenytoin, ciclosporin, calcium channel blockers); dry mouth
For example HIV or chemotherapy: faster breakdown
teach.caption: 'Linked with' means associated, not proven to cause. Healthy gums support general health, and the dental team is a route into wider healthcare.

teach.body: Update the medical history at every course of treatment, including any diabetes and how well it's controlled, and all medicines. Record smoking status and how much, exactly as the patient tells you. Record plaque and bleeding scores as the dentist instructs. Give very brief advice on smoking and signpost to local NHS stop-smoking services. Pass anything new, such as a new diagnosis or medicine, to the dentist. Accurate records let the dentist judge risk and explain why treatment may not work as well.

teach.text: Pale gums that barely bleed in a smoker do NOT mean healthy gums. Smoking masks bleeding and redness while bone loss continues. The classic exam answer: smoking reduces the signs of inflammation but worsens the disease.

items: Plaque is the primary cause; risk factors change how severely the body reacts.
Smoking is the biggest modifiable risk factor: it masks bleeding, worsens destruction and impairs healing.
Poorly controlled diabetes worsens periodontitis, and periodontitis worsens glucose control.
Highest risk: smoking plus poor plaque control, with irregular attendance.
Periodontitis is linked with cardiovascular disease, pregnancy outcomes and respiratory infection.
Record smoking, diabetes control and medicines accurately at every course of treatment.

summary: You can now explain why plaque causes periodontal disease but risk factors decide its severity, describe how smoking masks the signs while worsening the disease, explain the two-way link with diabetes, list other risk factors and systemic links, and record risk factors accurately.

A.q: Which is the biggest modifiable risk factor for periodontitis?
A.why: Smoking is the most important risk factor a patient can change: it worsens destruction and impairs healing.

whyNot.0: Age can't be changed, so it isn't modifiable.
whyNot.3: Sex can't be changed, so it isn't modifiable.

A.q: A heavy smoker has deep pockets and bone loss, but his gums barely bleed on probing. Why?
A.why: Smoking narrows the gum's blood vessels, so there is less bleeding and redness even though disease is advanced.

whyNot.0: Smoking doesn't kill plaque bacteria; smokers often have worse disease.
whyNot.1: Smoking slows healing rather than speeding it up.
whyNot.3: Staining is on the teeth and can't hide bleeding from the gums.

A.q: How does poorly controlled diabetes affect periodontal disease?
options: It has no real effect on the gums
A.why: Poorly controlled diabetes alters the immune response and slows healing, so periodontitis is more severe.

whyNot.1: Reduced bleeding is a smoking effect, not a diabetes effect.
whyNot.2: Diabetes is one of the best-known systemic risk factors for periodontitis.

B.q: Two patients have similar plaque levels but very different amounts of bone loss. Which factor most likely explains the difference?
B.why: Smoking changes the body's response to plaque, causing more bone loss for the same amount of plaque.

whyNot.1: A soft toothbrush is recommended and doesn't cause bone loss.
whyNot.2: Fluoride toothpaste protects against caries and doesn't affect bone loss.
whyNot.3: Drinking water doesn't explain differences in periodontal destruction.

B.q: Which patient is at the HIGHEST risk of periodontal breakdown?
options: A non-smoker with good plaque control
A smoker with excellent plaque control
A smoker with poor plaque control
B.why: Smoking combined with poor plaque control is the highest-risk combination: lots of plaque plus an impaired response to it.

whyNot.0: A non-smoker with good plaque control is at low risk.
whyNot.1: Good plaque control lowers a smoker's risk, though it remains higher than a non-smoker's.
whyNot.3: Regular attendance helps catch disease early and lowers risk.

B.q: Which statement about periodontitis and diabetes is correct?
options: Each condition can worsen the other
Diabetes affects teeth but not gums
B.why: The link is two-way: poorly controlled diabetes worsens periodontitis, and periodontal inflammation makes glucose harder to control.

whyNot.0: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition, not caused by gum disease.
whyNot.2: Diabetes is a major risk factor for gum disease.
whyNot.3: Successful periodontal treatment can help improve glucose control.

C.q: When should a patient's smoking status be recorded?
options: Only at the patient's first ever visit
Only if they ask for advice
Only if gum disease is found
C.why: Smoking habits change, so status should be checked and recorded whenever the medical history is updated.

whyNot.0: Patients may start or stop smoking after their first visit.
whyNot.1: Recording risk factors is routine, not just on request.
whyNot.2: Smoking affects many conditions, including oral cancer risk, so it is always recorded.

C.q: Periodontitis has been linked (associated) with which of these conditions?
C.why: Periodontitis is associated with cardiovascular disease, as well as diabetes and adverse pregnancy outcomes.

whyNot.1: Migraine is not a recognised periodontal link.
whyNot.2: Glaucoma is an eye condition with no recognised periodontal link.
whyNot.3: Hay fever is an allergy with no recognised periodontal link.

C.q: Which medicine group is associated with gum overgrowth, making plaque control harder?
C.why: Calcium channel blockers (such as nifedipine and amlodipine) can cause gingival overgrowth, as can phenytoin and ciclosporin.

whyNot.0: Proton pump inhibitors reduce stomach acid and are not linked with gum overgrowth.
whyNot.1: Statins lower cholesterol and are not linked with gum overgrowth.
whyNot.3: Antihistamines may dry the mouth but don't cause gum overgrowth.

reteach.title: A smoke alarm with the batteries out
reteach.question: What happens if a fire starts in a house where someone has taken the batteries out of the smoke alarm?

blocks.h: The alarm is silent, but the fire is burning
blocks.body: Bleeding gums are the mouth's smoke alarm: they warn that inflammation is happening. Smoking is like taking the batteries out. The alarm goes quiet (less bleeding, paler gums), but the fire carries on, and smoking makes it burn hotter (more bone loss, poorer healing). Poorly controlled diabetes is like leaving the windows open: the fire spreads faster, and the fire in turn makes the house harder to manage. Plaque is the spark in every case.

steps.label: Risk factors
steps.sub: Smoking, poor diabetes control, poor cleaning

explain.body: Plaque bacteria are the primary cause of periodontal disease. Risk factors such as smoking and poorly controlled diabetes don't cause it on their own; they change how severely the body reacts.

test.q: What is the primary cause of periodontal disease?
test.why: Plaque bacteria cause periodontal disease; the other factors modify how severe it becomes.

whyNot.0: Smoking is a major risk factor but not the cause.
whyNot.2: Diabetes is a risk factor that worsens the response to plaque.
whyNot.3: Stress is a risk factor, not the cause.

explain.body: Smoking narrows gum blood vessels and weakens immune defence. Gums bleed less and look paler while pockets deepen and bone is lost. Smokers also heal more slowly after treatment.

test.q: Why can smoking make periodontitis look less severe than it really is?
options: It removes plaque from the teeth
test.why: Reduced blood flow means less bleeding and redness, hiding the inflammation while destruction continues.

whyNot.2: Smoking weakens, rather than strengthens, the periodontal tissues.
whyNot.3: Smoking stains teeth; it doesn't whiten them.

explain.body: Poorly controlled diabetes makes periodontitis more likely and more severe. Periodontal inflammation in turn makes glucose harder to control. Better diabetes control lowers periodontal risk.

test.q: A patient's diabetes has recently become much better controlled. What effect would you expect on his periodontal risk?
test.why: Well-controlled diabetes carries much less periodontal risk than poorly controlled diabetes.

whyNot.0: Better control improves immune response and healing, so risk shouldn't rise.
whyNot.1: Diabetes control directly affects periodontal risk.
whyNot.3: Age is one factor, but diabetes control matters a great deal.

explain.body: Update the medical history at every course of treatment. Record smoking status and amount, diabetes and its control, and all medicines, exactly as the patient reports. Tell the dentist about anything new.

test.q: A patient tells you he has swapped smoking for vaping and has just been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. What should you do?
options: Note it only if he has gum disease
Leave the records until next year
Advise him to stop his diabetes tablets
Update the records and tell the dentist
test.why: Changes in smoking habits and medical history must be recorded accurately and passed to the dentist, as they affect risk and care.

whyNot.0: Risk factors are recorded for every patient, not just those with disease.
whyNot.1: Records must be kept up to date at each visit.
whyNot.2: Advising on prescribed medicines is outside your role and could be dangerous.
